Info for new candidates
A warm welcome to our doctoral community! This page contains everything you need to know as you set off on your doctoral adventure at the University of Auckland, joining more than 3,000 talented candidates from all over the world in pursuit of research excellence and impact.
On this page:
Key action points
Before you start
What to do on day 1
Get to know the University
Support for international candidates
Understanding your candidature
Frequently asked questions
Key action points
Doctoral Induction
You should attend the central Doctoral Induction within the first two months of enrolling as a doctoral candidate. We recommend you book as soon as possible. Note: If you have access to Wahapū, book via the Doctoral what's on page. If you do not have access to Wahapū, book via the Doctoral Event Registration Form.
Log into Wahapū
Wahapū is a comprehensive digital system for managing doctoral candidature, used by doctoral candidates, supervisors, academic heads, and all other parties involved in managing doctoral processes. All staff and new PhD candidates on the current PhD Statute are given automatic access, normally in the first few days of candidature, and you can log in using single sign-on. Learn more about Wahapū, log in, and access support pages on our About Wahapū page. Note: If you're studying towards a named doctorate (DClinPsy, DHSc, DMedSc, DocFA, EdD), you do not have access to Wahapū, but will manage your candidature using doctoral forms.
Canvas modules
Completing the Doctoral Candidature Essentials Canvas Course is an essential part of your onboarding. It includes seven modules:
Preparing for your Confirmation Review
Academic and Research Integrity
Managing your Candidature
Navigating Online Resources
Working with Supervisors
Doctoral Development
PhD Examination Process
GenAI Essentials
Before you start
Initial doctoral enrolment: Once you accept your unconditional offer of a place in a doctoral programme at the University of Auckland, you are then registered into your programme. Learn more about initial doctoral enrolment.
Scholarships: If you have been offered a scholarship, you need to inform a scholarship administrator that you have started your doctoral programme as soon as you enrol so that they can activate payments. If you have a University of Auckland Doctoral Scholarship, you can contact the University's Scholarships Office.
Supervisors: Let your supervisors know in advance about your start date so that desk space can be allocated and IT onboarding can be initiated. And if you haven't already done so, make an appointment for your first supervision meeting with them as soon as possible after enrolment. You can find out helpful tips about how to navigate the supervisor-candidate relationship in our Canvas module about Working with Supervisors.
What to do on day 1
Campus card: You can collect your campus card from the University's Student Hubs on City Campus or Grafton Campus. This ID card will allow you access to buildings and services. The Student Hubs can also help you with many of your other queries.
Doctoral Research Coordinator: Find out who your faculty/LSRI's Doctoral Research Coordinator is by asking your supervisors or emailing the addresses listed on our Doctoral contacts page.
Resources: You can speak to your Doctoral Research Coordinator about arranging resources such as your desk, laptop, printing, and office keys. It's also a good idea to familiarise yourself with the Doctoral Candidates - Resources Policy, which provides details of additional resources available to you.
Group Services: Introduce yourself to the Group Services team in your faculty/LSRI and find out about the admin roles they perform. Learn more on the Support for research students page.
Email address: Learn more about setting up your student email (userID@aucklanduni.ac.nz) so you don't miss out on important information. You may need the VPN service if you're connecting from off-campus. If you have queries, contact the Student IT Hub. In addition, we recommend you request a staff-type email address (firstname.lastname@auckland.ac.nz) from the Group Services team in your faculty/LSRI so you can access Open Access Publishing.
Get to know the University
Campus maps: If you're new to Auckland, the University's campus maps are very helpful.
IT queries: For basic IT queries, you can contact the Student IT Hub. For more complex IT questions, you can raise a ticket via the Staff Service Centre's IT Service Portal. Note: Depending on when you join the doctoral programme, there may be a delay of a few weeks before you gain access to certain resources such as the Staff Intranet and start to receive the fortnightly Doctoral News e-newsletter.
Health Services: Find out about enrolling with University Health and Counselling for comprehensive community healthcare, with information for domestic and international candidates.
Reach out for support and connection: Explore ways to make friends, join a club, or access support services by visiting the Doctoral wellbeing and community page for advice.
Accommodation: If you're looking for a place to stay, visit the University's accommodation web page to find out more.
Public transport: If you're planning to take the bus, train or ferry in Auckland, you can buy an Auckland Transport Hop Card which is valid for all modes of public transport. Learn more at AT Hop Card.
Parking: If you have a car and will be driving to campus, you may like to explore the car parking options for staff that are also available to doctoral candidates. There are also options for bike and scooter parking.
Support for international candidates
International students: The University's International Office offers a wide variety of support for international students. You can learn more at International student support or contact the team at int-questions@auckland.ac.nz. There is also helpful visa information on the Continuing PhD candidates page.|
English support: If English is not your first language, you can find support options on the English language support and Academic English Hub pages.
Understanding your candidature
Confirmation Milestones: Attending a Doctoral Induction is one of the first milestones you must complete in the first year of your doctorate, in order to be confirmed into the programme. Learn more about the other milestones on our Confirmation web page.
Confirmation support: You should aim to complete the online PhD Confirmation of Candidature module in the Doctoral Candidature Essentials Canvas Course within the first two months of enrolling. This, together with the Doctoral Induction, will provide you with the knowledge and tools you need for a successful provisional year.
Understand your enrolment and fees: Your enrolment lasts for 12 months from your start date. You can view your fees at Student Services Online. If you're an international student, make sure you know how the  domestic fee policy works. Learn more about Doctoral fees and Paying your fees.
Coursework enrolment: If you are a doctoral candidate who needs an enrolment in coursework as part of your doctoral confirmation milestones, or needs a change in an existing enrolment in any approved confirmation milestone course, you should under no circumstances attempt to enrol yourself in coursework, or modify an existing coursework enrolment using Student Services Online. Learn what you should do in Doctoral coursework enrolment and changes.
Policies: Visit our Doctoral Policies web page to explore more key doctoral policies. You'll also find a link to the University's Policy Hub.
PReSS: Postgraduate Research Student Support (PReSS) funding is provided by the University to assist with the provision of financial support for doctoral research that is not funded by other sources. Learn more about your PReSS account so you can start planning how best to spend your budget.
Research resources: Explore the comprehensive Research resources pages to find services, resources and people to accelerate your research.
ResearchSpace: It's hard to write a thesis if you've never read one, so we recommend exploring ResearchSpace (the University's digital thesis repository) and having a look through a few doctoral theses from your field of study.
